text.en: The school bell rang and Navya walked with her grandfather, Dada ji, to the bus stop. On the bus ride home they passed a postbox, a metro train, a flyover, a hospital and a bank with an ATM, and Dada ji explained each one. By the time Navya reached home she had learnt how letters travelled, how money is kept safe and how to draw a map of her neighbourhood. Let us ride along and explore.

Navya saw a red postbox on the corner and Dada ji told her that he used to write letters to his brother who studied in another city. The letter is dropped into the postbox, then the postman takes it to the post office. The post office sorts the letters by region and sends them to their destinations. Post offices offer other services too, like sending parcels and important documents. You can write a letter to a friend and post it, and you will feel the joy of sending and receiving a letter.
Long ago people communicated using drumbeats and carvings on rocks. Later, letters were carried by messengers and even pigeons, and much later the postal service started. New inventions like the telephone, radio and television made it easier to share information. Today, mobile phones and computers with the internet let us connect with anyone, anywhere, in seconds. Dada ji said that in his time a reply could take weeks, but today messages and video calls are fast. But quick messages can also spread wrong news very fast, so before we share news we should check that it is true.
From the bus Navya saw a metro train racing by, and Dada ji said metro trains travel very fast. High roads called flyovers help vehicles go above busy roads and crossings, so they save travellers' time. Some flyovers are built for metros and others for buses and cars. These modern facilities make life easier, but many animals, birds and trees that lived there are no longer around. Dada ji said we can balance development and nature by planting trees to keep our environment secure.
The bus stopped near a hospital with a banner for an Eye Check-up Camp, and many people were going in. Dada ji explained that people come to a hospital when they are unwell, and he had brought Navya's grandmother here for her eye operation. A doctor treats patients and prescribes medicines, and a nurse looks after patients and helps the doctor. Other people who work in a hospital or health centre include pharmacists, lab workers and cleaners, and all of them are important.
Near home they passed a bank with an ATM, short for Automated Teller Machine, which helps us take out money whenever we need it. A bank is a special place where money is kept safe, and it also helps us save money for the future. Long ago, people had to stand in long queues at the bank and used Money Orders through the post office to send money. Today we can send money online by mobile phone within seconds, as Navya's uncle did for Raksha Bandhan. Long ago people used the barter system, for example a farmer exchanging wheat for a shepherd's milk, but it was hard to find the right partner and value, so money was invented. The first page of a bank passbook shows the account number, the customer's name and the branch.
Saving means keeping some of your money aside for later instead of spending all of it. If you get pocket money you can keep part in a piggy bank, and a plan or budget helps you decide how much to spend and how much to save. For example, if you have 100 rupees in a month you might plan to save 40 rupees and spend 60 rupees on stationery and snacks. Saving helps when you need something important later, or when something unexpected happens.
Navya sat down to draw her neighbourhood, and used the rising Sun to find East. On a map, North is shown at the top, South at the bottom, East on the right and West on the left. So a place to the east of her house goes on the right side of the paper, and a place to the north goes at the top. To describe a route to a friend you can use left, right, forward and backward, and landmarks like a park, a shop or a bus stop. Public places like hospitals, banks, post offices, police stations, libraries and bus stations give services that keep us healthy, safe and connected. Many helpers served our neighbourhood during COVID-19, such as doctors, nurses, garbage collectors, shopkeepers and teachers, and it is good to thank them.

problem.en: Navya has a school in the east and a park in the north. Where do you draw them on her map?

text.en: Remember the map rule: North up, South down, East right, West left.

why.en: This is the same on every map.

text.en: The school is in the east, so draw it on the right side of her house.
The park is in the north, so draw it at the top.

problem.en: You have 100 rupees for a month. Make a simple plan.

text.en: Decide a saving amount first, for example 40 rupees in the piggy bank.

why.en: Saving first makes sure it is not spent.

text.en: Spend the rest on needs, for example 60 rupees for stationery and a little for snacks.
Add the two amounts: 40 + 60 = 100.

prompt.en: Tell how the post office, the bank and the hospital each help people in a neighbourhood.

requiredIdeas.en: Post office sends letters and parcels
Bank keeps money safe and helps save
Hospital treats people who are unwell
They are public places that give services

commonMisconceptions.en: Letters reach on the same day always
A hospital is only for operations

points.en: The post office sorts and sends letters and parcels, and communication has become faster over time.
Metros and flyovers speed up travel but we must also protect trees and animals.
A bank keeps money safe and an ATM gives money; saving helps for the future.
On a map North is up, South is down, East is right and West is left.
Public places like hospitals and libraries give services that help the whole neighbourhood.
